original_question: Which gene is mutated in the autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth, and encodes a protein that indirectly inhibits RANKL (also known as tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11)?
key_entities: tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11

final_qi.question: Which gene is mutated in the autosomal recessive disorder characterized by bone overgrowth, and encodes a protein that indirectly inhibits RANKL (also known as tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11)?
final_qi.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive bone overgrowth disorder juvenile Paget disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TNFRSF11B gene. TNFRSF11B encodes osteoprotegerin, a soluble decoy receptor that binds to and neutralizes RANKL (tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11). By sequestering RANKL, osteoprotegerin indirectly inhibits the RANKL–RANK signaling pathway that drives osteoclast formation and bone resorption; when TNFRSF11B is mutated, this inhibition is lost, resulting in excessive bone turnover and skeletal overgrowth.

final_answer.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive bone-overgrowth disorder sclerosteosis is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene. SOST encodes sclerostin, an osteocyte-secreted protein that antagonizes Wnt/β-catenin signaling in osteoblasts. By dampening Wnt signaling, sclerostin lowers expression of RANKL (tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 11), thereby indirectly inhibiting RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis. Absence of functional SOST removes this brake, resulting in excessive bone formation and generalized skeletal overgrowth.
